To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the human thymic output is inversely proportional to age and that HIV infection is associated with a significant decline in thymic output, which is likely to be a major contributing factor in HIV-associated immune deficiency.
the thymus continues to produce T-cells throughout adult life, but the number of thymic emigrant T-cells decreases with age.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of thymopoiesic function and the mechanisms by which it is affected by age and HIV infection.
the development, function and regulation of the human immune system.
the role that the thymus plays in maintaining a competent immune system throughout the life span of an individual.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
thymopoiesic activity is maintained throughout the adult life and that HIV infection results in a profound thymic dysfunction.
the human thymic function is not a static organ and it is still capable of producing new T-cells throughout adult life.
the thymus does not stop functioning with age, but rather, its output decreases with age and is further reduced by HIV infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the human thymic microenvironment is a dynamic system that is capable of producing new thymocytes and is not a nonfunctional organ, as was once believed, and that HIV infection is capable of altering the thymic micro-environment in a manner that results in a net loss of T-cells.
the thymus remains a vital organ in the human body, which continues to produce naive T-cells throughout the adult life.
the human thymic inviolable is not a static entity but rather a dynamic organ that can be manipulated to enhance thymic function in an age- and HIV-associated context.
The main takeaway from our work is that
thymic output is not static and is highly responsive to the environment.
the thymus, despite its age, can still function to generate T-cells and that HIV infection can be detrimental in that process.
the thymus continues to function throughout adulthood and that HIV-mediated thymus dysfunction is a major factor in the immunodeficiency observed in HIV-infected patients.
